## Personality

Solemn, serious and proud; Neffa practises the long songs under her breath all day long.

## Lore

Neffa is ten years old and practises the long songs under her breath all day long: while she eats, while she sweeps, while she walks to the cisterns for water, and, according to her mother, while she sleeps. She is solemn, serious and proud, and she has a plan. Before she turns twelve, she will stand up at a gathering of the four families in the great hall and recite the whole long song of the Old Ones without a single mistake.

### Brenna House

Neffa is the daughter of Lessa, the best bonesetter in the highlands, and the granddaughter of Odda, chieftain of the Brenna, and Thrun, who beats the great drum that calls the families together. Her father, Corrick, was a Brenna storyteller with a gift for voices. He died of a lung fever when she was two, and she does not remember him, though everyone tells her she has his ear for rhythm. She keeps that like a treasure.

She grew up in Brenna House among herbs, drums and stories, and she has always been the quiet one in a loud household. Her grandfather laughs from the belly and drums the same way; her grandmother can settle any quarrel with a story; her mother scolds patients for muddy boots. Neffa listens to all of them and remembers everything they say, which has made her, at ten, a slightly alarming person to argue with.

### Ahvi's pupil

Four years ago, Ahvi, the family's song-keeper and Odda's cousin, heard six-year-old Neffa repeat an entire evening's singing back to her mother the next morning, and took her as a pupil the same day. Ahvi had been chosen the same way when she was a child, and she told Neffa so, which Neffa considers the most important thing anyone has ever told her.

The long song of the Old Ones names every Old One of Midbarium back to the Age of Division, with their families, their deeds and the chieftains who stood beside them. It takes most of a night to sing. Ahvi is a demanding teacher: after any mistake at all, however small, Neffa must go back to the very beginning. Neffa has never once complained. She has, however, kept a private count of how many times she has started over, scratched on the underside of her bed, and it is well into the hundreds.

She can now sing three-quarters of the song without a slip. The last quarter holds the most recent Old Ones, and she stumbles in the same place every time: the verse for Old One Varra, Ahvi's sister, who died when Neffa was four. Neffa remembers Varra, a little, as a big laugh at the end of a table, and she is not sure why that verse is the one that trips her. Ahvi has not told her that she, too, finds it the hardest to sing.

### The other verse

Neffa has noticed that Ahvi has been singing something alone in her room at night this summer, a short, strange verse from the oldest part of the song that Neffa has never been taught. She has heard enough of it through the wall to know it is about beasts. She has asked Ahvi about it once. Ahvi said it was not for learning yet, and Neffa, who has never been told that about any verse before, has not stopped thinking about it.

### What she wants

Neffa wants to recite the long song whole, before twelve, in front of everyone, and to see her grandmother pretend not to be proud. She fears stumbling in front of the families, and she fears, more quietly, that the song will one day have to name something she does not want it to.

A quest could help Neffa find the old meaning of a name or deed she cannot place in the song, or be in the great hall on the night she finally stands up to recite.
